Title: Two failed startups and one YC company later, here's what I'd do before founding again

My first two companies failed. My last one raised about $1.5M, including YC. Before starting again, this is what I'd do differently:

1. Trust your gut and take the fights early. I was too ready to let things go. Hard calls get harder the longer you wait.

2. Find people with backbone. My best early investors and hires challenged me. Healthy arguments saved the company more than once.

3. Stay small until customers tell you what to build. We spent too much on tech and on growth we expected but didn't have. Sell first, then build exactly what clients need.

4. Don't incorporate before you need to, and don't cheap out when you do. Our $250 online setup was almost entirely redone by a lawyer after we got into YC. I'd also set it up a year early, for nothing.

5. Mistakes I keep seeing: raising before you have network or traction, entering a market you don't know, cofounders you've never worked with, giving early investors 30–40%, and a valuation that's too high or too low.

Before anything, I now tell people to run five validations: market, tech, team, financial, legal. They're quick, and they tell you whether to keep going or stop.

Which of these did you learn the hard way?

posts.text:
I mentor founders at accelerators, and I led Founder Institute in Colombia as a volunteer. Every journey is different, but these mistakes come up again and again:

• Raising too early, without the network or the traction to make it work for you
• Going into a market where you have no context, no special insight and no network
• Starting with cofounders you've never worked with, when you already know people you trust
• Giving early investors 30–40% of the company, so there's no room left to raise the next round
• Raising at a valuation that's too high, or too low

If a friend told me tomorrow they were quitting to start something, I'd tell them to run five validations first: market, tech, team, financial, legal. They're usually quick.

posts.text:
Side project starting to look like a company? One thing I'd do differently: don't set up the company before you need it, and don't cheap out when you do.

For my last startup I used a US online service, about $250, and set it up a year to a year and a half before we really started. It looked fine. When we got into YC, a proper lawyer reviewed everything, and almost all of it had to be redone.

• Paying for a company you don't use yet, with paperwork you'll redo anyway, is the wrong order
• When you do set it up, have a lawyer look at it before the first cheque comes in, not after

My own experience, not legal advice.

posts.title: What I'd tell myself before founding a startup
posts.subtitle: Two failed companies, then one that raised about $1.5M including Y Combinator. Five lessons, and the mistakes I see founders make most.
posts.text:
Being a founder is a bit like an STD: once you have it, you never get rid of it. My first company was in high school. It failed. The second was in crypto, while I studied in London. That failed too. My last one raised about $1.5M, including Y Combinator.

Along the way I led Founder Institute in Colombia as a volunteer, and I still mentor at accelerators. This is what I'd tell myself before starting again, and what I'd tell any founder I mentor.

1. Trust your gut, and take the fights early

By the time I started, I'd been grinding for years. I was too ready to let things go, too ready to think "I've worked hard enough, success should come now." If I did it again, I'd be braver: make the hard decisions quickly, and take the fights while they're still small.

In Colombia there's a phrase, malicia indígena: the street smarts to know that not everyone has your best interests at heart. Most people are fine, but you will meet some who aren't. Better to expect it than to learn it late.

2. Find people with backbone

The best thing I did was find a few really good people: some investors, some early employees. Honest, hard-working, sharing my values, and with enough backbone to challenge me. We had healthy arguments, and nothing would have happened without them. Look for people who will tell you you're wrong.

3. Stay small until customers tell you what to build

I spent almost a year trying things and looking for the right people to start with. Then the money came in steps:

  1. $70k from the first investors
  2. $200k from angels
  3. $500k from Y Combinator
  4. About $700–800k more on the back of YC

Roughly $1.5M in total. Too much of it went on tech, and on the growth we expected instead of the growth we had. We should have stayed small and focused on sales and on working with clients. Once the clients showed us what to build, we should have hired for exactly that, or hacked it together ourselves. We didn't, and that's 100% on me.

4. Don't set up the company before you need it, and don't cheap out when you do

We used a US online service to set up the company for about $250. It looked fine. It wasn't. When we got into YC, a proper lawyer reviewed everything, and almost all of it had to be redone.

Worse, I'd set it up a year to a year and a half before we really started. Paying for a company you don't use yet, with paperwork you'll redo anyway, is the wrong order. When you do set it up, have a lawyer look at it before the first cheque comes in, not after.

5. The mistakes I see most

  1. Raising too early, without the network, the traction or anything else that makes it work for you.
  2. Going into a market where you have no context, no special insight and no network to lean on.
  3. Starting with cofounders you've never worked with, when you already know people you trust.
  4. Giving early investors 30–40% of the company. Then there isn't enough room left to raise the next round.
  5. Raising at a valuation that's too high, or too low.

What I'd tell a friend who's quitting tomorrow

Run five validations first: market, tech, people, financial and legal. They're usually quick. Whether you do them now or six months in, they're what tell you whether to keep going or stop. So the sooner you check them off, the better.

I'm building Capfolder now, a free, open-source cap table app. The full guide: https://capfolder.com/guides/before-you-found/

I'm not a lawyer, and this isn't legal, tax or financial advice. It's my own experience.

Which of these did you learn the hard way?
